items.title: The store and accounts
items.text: Razer deactivated every account on June 25, 2019. Its notice said funds left in accounts “may be turned over to the applicable authority,” and that downloaded games would keep working only if they did not validate a purchase at launch.[^30][^32]

items.title: The hardware
items.text: Razer said in 2015 that it was “not retaining interest in OUYA hardware or related other assets.”[^25] What happened to those assets, and to Ouya, Inc. itself, is not in our sources.

items.title: The name
items.text: Razer’s 2015 press release said it planned to publish Android TV games “under the OUYA moniker as a separate interest.”[^25] We found no product released under the name after the 2019 shutdown, and we have not checked who holds the trademark registration today.

items.title: The team
items.text: The technical and developer-relations staff joined Razer’s software team in 2015 to work on its Forge TV platform, whose store closed on the same day as Ouya’s.[^25][^30]

items.title: The developers’ fund
items.text: Razer said it would honour the **$620,000** still unpaid from the Free the Games Fund, to some 27 developers, dropping exclusivity and asking for free copies for its own store’s users instead.[^27][^28] Whether every developer was paid is not in our sources.

items.title: The consoles
items.text: A community-written replacement server lets an Ouya sign in and install games again after the official shutdown, by pointing the console at a new address in a configuration file. It is a static stand-in, stores no user data and takes no payments.[^35]

items.title: TowerFall
items.text: The game that sold about 7,000 copies on Ouya reached $500,000 in revenue after moving to PlayStation 4 and PC.[^21]

blocks.title: Who has owned the Ouya name
blocks.subtitle: One sale, of the software and the name without the box.

nodes.what: Raises $8,596,474 on Kickstarter for a $99 Android console.[^1]
Kleiner Perkins leads a $15M round with Mayfield, Nvidia, Shasta and Occam. Venture debt from TriplePoint follows.[^8][^24]

nodes.owner: Ouya, with Alibaba as an investor
nodes.what: Alibaba invests to bring the catalogue to its set-top box in China.[^23]
A debt covenant is tripped and a bank is hired to find a buyer.[^24]
Acquires the content catalogue, the online store and the team. Not the hardware.[^25]
Shuts down the store, accounts and website.[^30]

nodes.owner: No known user of the name
nodes.what: Nothing is sold as Ouya. Volunteers run a replacement server for old consoles.[^35] The trademark’s current status is unknown to us.

blocks.source: Kickstarter[^1], PocketGamer.biz[^8][^23], Fortune[^24], Razer[^25][^30] and Engadget[^26]. Ouya did not go through bankruptcy as far as our sources show; the red markers denote the forced sale and the shutdown.
